title: Saudi Arabia | SAMA Cyber Security Framework and Information Protection
tagline: Apply SAMA's cyber security, awareness, branch control and cyber-fraud rules as a member of staff at a conventional Saudi bank.
sectors: Conventional commercial banks in Saudi Arabia
Foreign bank branches in Saudi Arabia
Bank call centres and outsourced service providers
IT and cyber security service providers to Saudi banks
description:
This quest teaches the cyber security and information protection rules the **Saudi Central Bank (SAMA)** sets for conventional banks. It is based on SAMA's **Cyber Security Framework** (2017), in particular sections 3.1.6 (awareness) and 3.1.7 (training), roles, risk management and incident management; the **Information Technology Governance Framework** (2021) on IT staff competence; the **Business Continuity Management Framework** in general terms; the **Counter-Fraud Framework** (2022) where it deals with cyber-enabled fraud; the **Control and Awareness Measures for Branch and Customer Service Employees** (2021); and SAMA's instructions on the **Personal Data Protection Law**, all published in the SAMA Rulebook.

SAMA requires every bank to run an approved cyber security awareness programme for staff, third parties and customers through the year and to measure it, to give specialist training to key roles, and to run information security and fraud campaigns for branch and customer service staff at least every three months, with tests at least every six months. This quest supports those duties for all bank staff, with extra depth for branch, customer service, IT, cyber and fraud teams.

The quest builds knowledge and does not replace your bank's own policies, procedures or the latest SAMA instructions; always follow them. The Personal Data Protection Law is covered only in general terms. The quest covers conventional banking only.
audience: All employees of conventional banks in Saudi Arabia, as part of the bank's cyber security awareness programme
Branch, teller and customer service staff, including contracted call-centre agents
IT staff, developers, administrators and risk assessors who need specialist cyber skills
Cyber security, counter-fraud, compliance and internal audit staff who run or check the programme
outcomes: Explain the structure, governance roles and maturity model of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework
Design and evaluate awareness and training that meets sections 3.1.6 and 3.1.7 and the IT staff competence rules
Recognise phishing, whaling and other social-engineering attacks and apply SAMA's counter-fraud safeguards
Apply SAMA's 2021 branch controls: passwords, need-to-know access, logs, campaigns, tests and declarations
Follow SAMA's risk management and incident notification rules and link them to business continuity
Assemble the evidence a SAMA cyber review expects

quest.name: The Citadel of Trust
quest.premise: You have just joined Rimal Bank, a fictional conventional bank headquartered in Riyadh, as Cyber Security Awareness Officer. A phishing simulation has gone badly, a Jeddah customer has lost savings to a caller posing as the bank, and SAMA will review the bank's cyber self-assessment this quarter. With CISO Lama Al-Mutairi, SOC lead Priya Raman, branch manager Omar Bakr, customer service officer Hessa Al-Shammari and counter-fraud head Yousef Haddad, clear five stages, then face the final boss: the SAMA reviewer's exam.

sessions.title: SAMA's Cyber Security Framework: Governance, Roles and Maturity
sessions.summary: Meet SAMA's 2017 Cyber Security Framework: its scope, four domains and maturity model, and who owns cyber security at a Saudi bank, from the board and cyber committee to the CISO and every member of staff.

Describe the governance set-up SAMA expects: board, cyber committee, independent cyber function and CISO

cards.title: Day one in the CISO office
cards.setting: Cyber Security Department, Rimal Bank head office, Olaya, Riyadh. 8:15 am.

lines.text: You have just joined Rimal Bank, a fictional conventional bank with branches from Jeddah to Al-Khobar, as Cyber Security Awareness Officer.
Welcome! I'm Lama Al-Mutairi, the bank's CISO. Your timing is perfect: SAMA will review our Cyber Security Framework self-assessment this quarter.
Priya Raman, SOC lead. Bad news first: last week's phishing simulation. Forty-one staff clicked the link and nine typed their passwords.
Omar Bakr, branch manager in Al-Khobar. Some of those were my tellers. They say nobody ever trained them on this.
Yousef Haddad, Counter-Fraud. And a customer in Jeddah lost savings to a caller who claimed to be from our bank.
So the board will ask one question: is our awareness programme real, or is it a poster on the wall?
We start at the Citadel Gate: how SAMA's framework is built and who owns cyber security. Ready?

cards.title: SAMA's Cyber Security Framework in one minute

scenes.heading: One framework for the sector
scenes.narration: SAMA issued its Cyber Security Framework by circular in May 2017. Every bank operating in Saudi Arabia must adopt it, and it replaced SAMA's earlier cyber security circulars.

scenes.heading: What it protects
scenes.narration: The goal is the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information assets: electronic and paper information, applications, devices such as ATMs, storage media, premises and networks.

scenes.heading: Principle based
scenes.narration: For each topic the framework sets a principle, an objective and control considerations. Where a control cannot be applied, the bank looks at compensating controls, internal risk acceptance and a formal waiver request to SAMA.

scenes.heading: Self-assessment
scenes.narration: Banks assess themselves periodically against a questionnaire, and SAMA reviews and audits those self-assessments to judge compliance and maturity.

scenes.heading: Maturity
scenes.narration: Maturity is scored from level 0 to level 5. SAMA expects member organisations to operate at level 3 or higher: controls defined, approved, implemented and monitored.

cards.title: Four domains of the framework
cards.caption: All domains apply to banks. Awareness (3.1.6) and training (3.1.7) sit in the first domain, next to governance.

items.label: Domain 1
items.right: Governance, strategy, policy, roles, projects, awareness, training

items.label: Domain 2
items.right: Risk process, regulatory compliance, industry standards, reviews, audits

items.label: Domain 3
items.right: HR, access, applications, e-banking, events, incidents, threats

cards.question: Which statement about the scope of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework is accurate?
options: It covers only systems connected to the internet
It covers electronic and physical information, devices, applications, premises and networks
It applies to banks only after SAMA approves a bank's opt-in request
It replaces the bank's fraud and physical security policies entirely
cards.explanation: The framework lists electronic and hard-copy information, applications, machines such as ATMs, storage media, premises and networks. It links to fraud and physical security policies but does not replace their non-cyber parts.

cards.title: The documentation pyramid at maturity level 3
cards.caption: Level 3 means the controls are written down, approved, implemented and monitored, with KPIs reported.

items.label: Policy: why
items.detail: Board-endorsed. Says why cyber security matters and what must be protected.

items.label: Standards: what
items.detail: Baselines such as password rules, segregation of duties, logging and backups.

items.label: Procedures: how
items.detail: Step-by-step tasks for staff, third parties and customers.

cards.title: Who owns cyber security at a Saudi bank
cards.body:
The framework is clear that **the board carries ultimate responsibility**. It may delegate work to a **cyber security committee**, but not the accountability.

- **Committee:** mandated by the board, headed by an **independent senior manager from a control function**, with the CISO and senior managers (for example COO, CIO, compliance) as members. Internal audit may sit in as an observer. The charter sets a minimum meeting frequency of **quarterly**.
- **Cyber security function:** independent of IT, with separate reporting lines, budgets and staff evaluations. It reports to the CEO or managing director, or to the general manager of a control function.
- **CISO:** a full-time senior manager, who must be a **Saudi national**, sufficiently qualified, and appointed only after SAMA gives **no objection**.
- **Senior management:** makes sure staff accept and follow the policy and that cyber duties appear in job descriptions of key positions.
- **Internal audit:** performs cyber security audits.
- **Every member of staff:** complies with the cyber security policy, standards and procedures.

cards.title: Roles under section 3.1.4
cards.prompt: Match each role to a responsibility the framework gives it.

pairs.right: Ultimate responsibility; allocates budget and endorses the strategy and policy
Approves and monitors programmes such as awareness, plus cyber KRIs and KPIs
Defines and runs the awareness programmes and oversees incident investigations
Puts cyber duties into job descriptions of key positions and staff
Performs cyber security audits
Comply with the cyber security policy, standards and procedures

cards.title: A shortcut on the org chart
cards.setting: CISO office, Rimal Bank, Riyadh. Later that morning.

lines.text: Lama, a thought. Wouldn't it be simpler if cyber security just reported to the CIO? Same building, same systems.
Simpler, yes. But SAMA wants the cyber function independent of IT: its own reporting line, budget and staff evaluations.
Otherwise the team that builds the systems also grades its own security homework.
Fair. And who checks that the awareness programme actually works?
The CISO runs it, the committee approves and monitors it, and internal audit tests it. Let's see how you would handle a real board proposal.

cards.title: The cost-saving proposal
cards.situation: A board member at Rimal Bank proposes saving money by merging the cyber security function into the IT department under the CIO, and letting the CIO's deputy act as CISO part-time. The chief executive asks you for a one-line view before the board meets.

choices.text: Advise that the proposal conflicts with SAMA's framework: the cyber function must stay independent of IT, and the CISO must be a full-time senior manager approved by SAMA.
choices.outcome: Best answer. Section 3.1.1 calls for an independent function with separate reporting lines, budgets and evaluations, and a full-time CISO who is Saudi, qualified and appointed only after SAMA's no objection.

choices.text: Accept the merger but ask the CIO to send SAMA a yearly report on cyber security.
choices.outcome: A report does not cure the conflict of interest. The framework requires structural independence, not just reporting.

choices.text: Accept the merger for now and request a SAMA waiver later if inspectors raise it.
choices.outcome: Waivers exist for control considerations that cannot be applied, with compensating controls and risk acceptance. Choosing to break a governance requirement to save money is not that situation.

choices.text: Suggest keeping the function separate but letting the CISO role be part-time.
choices.outcome: Half right. Independence is kept, but the framework calls for a full-time senior manager as CISO.

cards.back: SAMA's term for the regulated institutions that must adopt the framework, including every bank operating in the Kingdom.
A numbered control the framework mandates for a subdomain; the bank should apply it to reach the objective.
A formal request to SAMA when a control cannot be applied, after compensating controls and internal risk acceptance are considered.
Structured and formalised: controls defined, approved, implemented and monitored, with KPIs.
Managed and measurable: effectiveness is measured with KRIs and improved.
Confidentiality, integrity and availability of information assets, the three objectives of cyber security.

cards.title: Whose job is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each task to the role the framework gives it.

items.text: Allocate sufficient budget for cyber security
Approve the cyber security committee charter
Define and conduct the awareness programmes
Gather and analyse threat intelligence
Measure and report cyber KRIs and KPIs
Follow the password standard every day
Comply with cyber policy, standards and procedures

cards.title: Real case: SAMA's banking sector cyber strategy (2017)
cards.body:
In **March 2017**, two months before the framework itself, SAMA published an **Information Security Strategy for the Banking Sector** in its Rulebook. SAMA's foreword explained why: public disclosures showed cyber attacks rising in number, impact and sophistication, globally and in the region, and cyber incidents can cross borders and disturb financial stability.

The strategy prepares the sector across **five domains: identify, protect, detect, respond and recover**, with an emphasis on threat intelligence and collaboration between SAMA and the banks. One of its aims is a sector-wide cyber security **education programme and awareness campaign**.

**Lesson for you:** the awareness duty in section 3.1.6 is not a stand-alone rule. It is part of a sector plan in which every bank's staff, contractors and customers are a line of defence. When you design Rimal Bank's programme, you are delivering one piece of that national strategy.

*Source: SAMA Rulebook, Information Security Strategy for the Banking Sector (1438H / 2017).*

cards.title: SAMA's maturity scale
cards.caption: A bank must meet every criterion of the lower levels before it can claim a higher one.

items.label: Level 0: Non-existent
items.detail: No documentation, no awareness, no controls.

items.label: Level 1: Ad hoc
items.detail: Controls partly defined and applied inconsistently.

items.label: Level 2: Repeatable but informal
items.detail: Standard practice, but not written down or approved.

items.label: Level 3: Structured and formalised
items.detail: Defined, approved, implemented, monitored with KPIs. SAMA's minimum expectation.

items.label: Level 4: Managed and measurable
items.detail: Effectiveness measured with KRIs and improved.

items.label: Level 5: Adaptive
items.detail: Continuous improvement, linked to enterprise risk, benchmarked against peers.

cards.question: Rimal Bank runs a phishing awareness email every month, but nothing is written down or approved and no one measures the results. At what maturity level does this activity sit?
options: Level 4: managed and measurable
Level 2: repeatable but informal
Level 3: structured and formalised
Level 5: adaptive
cards.explanation: A standard, repeated practice that is not formally defined or approved is level 2. Level 3 needs the programme defined, approved, implemented and monitored with KPIs.

cards.title: Citadel Gate: what to remember
items: SAMA's Cyber Security Framework (May 2017) applies to every bank in the Kingdom, and all four domains apply to banks.
The board holds ultimate responsibility; a committee headed by an independent senior manager from a control function meets at least quarterly.
The cyber function is independent of IT, and the CISO is a full-time Saudi senior manager appointed after SAMA's no objection.
Banks self-assess periodically; SAMA reviews them and expects at least maturity level 3.
The cyber policy must include an awareness programme, and every member of staff must comply with policy, standards and procedures.

cards.prompt: Think about your own bank: could you name the CISO, the committee that approves the awareness programme and the place where your own cyber duties are written? Which of these would you struggle to find?

quiz.question: When did SAMA issue its Cyber Security Framework, and what happened to its earlier cyber circulars?
options: March 2015; they remain in force alongside it
November 2021; they were merged into the IT framework
May 2017; the framework superseded them
October 2022; they now apply only to finance companies
quiz.explanation: The framework was issued by circular dated May 2017 and states that it supersedes SAMA's previously issued cyber security circulars.

quiz.question: Which three objectives does the framework use to define cyber security?
options: Confidentiality, integrity and availability
Prevention, detection and prosecution
Identity, authentication and authorisation
Governance, compliance and audit
quiz.explanation: The framework's general security objectives are confidentiality, integrity and availability of information assets.

quiz.question: A bank cannot apply one control consideration because of a legacy core system. What route does the framework describe?
options: Skip the control silently, since the framework is only guidance
Ask the vendor to certify the system as compliant instead
Report the gap in the next annual financial statements
Apply compensating controls, accept the risk internally and request a formal waiver from SAMA
quiz.explanation: Section 2.2 says that where a control cannot be applied the bank should consider compensating controls, internal risk acceptance and a formal waiver request to SAMA.

quiz.question: What minimum maturity level does SAMA expect member organisations to reach?
options: Level 1, ad hoc
Level 2, repeatable but informal
Level 5, adaptive
Level 3, structured and formalised
quiz.explanation: The framework says member organisations should at least operate at maturity level 3 or higher.

quiz.question: Who should head Rimal Bank's cyber security committee?
options: The Chief Information Officer
An independent senior manager from a control function
The head of internal audit
An external consultant chosen by the board
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.1 says the committee should be headed by an independent senior manager from a control function. Internal audit may attend only as an observer.

quiz.question: Which condition must be met before a bank appoints its CISO?
options: SAMA must give its no objection to the appointment
The CISO must have ten years at the same bank
The board must hold a shareholder vote
The CISO must also chair the IT steering committee
quiz.explanation: The framework requires the CISO to be a Saudi national, sufficiently qualified, and appointed only after SAMA's no objection.

quiz.question: The IT director proposes that the cyber team share IT's budget and be evaluated by IT managers. Why does this conflict with the framework?
options: The framework bans cyber staff from working in the same building as IT
Only the board may evaluate cyber security staff
The cyber function must have separate reporting lines, budgets and staff evaluations from IT
Budgets for cyber security must be approved by SAMA each year
quiz.explanation: To avoid conflicts of interest, section 3.1.1 requires the cyber function to be independent of IT with separate reporting lines, budgets and evaluations.

quiz.question: Under section 3.1.4, which body approves and monitors cyber security programmes such as the awareness programme?
options: The cyber security committee
The internal audit function
The human resources department
The SAMA IT risk supervision team
quiz.explanation: The committee approves, communicates, supports and monitors cyber programmes, including awareness, and the cyber KRIs and KPIs. The CISO defines and runs them.

quiz.question: What must the bank's cyber security policy say about awareness?
options: That awareness is optional for staff who do not use computers
That awareness is delivered only after a cyber incident
That customers are excluded from awareness activity
That relevant stakeholders are made aware of cyber security and their expected behaviour
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.3 lists, among the policy's requirements, that relevant stakeholders are made aware of cyber security and expected behaviour through an awareness programme.

quiz.question: How often, at a minimum, should the cyber security committee meet according to its charter requirements?
options: Monthly
Quarterly
Twice a year
Annually
quiz.explanation: The committee charter must reflect a meeting frequency with a minimum of quarterly meetings.

sessions.title: Awareness and Training under Sections 3.1.6 and 3.1.7
sessions.summary: Build an awareness programme SAMA would recognise: three audiences, tailored content, activity through the year and measured effectiveness, plus specialist cyber training, IT staff competence and continuity awareness.
objectives: Apply the awareness requirements of section 3.1.6 to staff, third parties and customers
Identify the groups that need specialist training under section 3.1.7 and the HR-related duties in section 3.3.1
Describe the IT staff competence and training rules of SAMA's IT Governance Framework
Choose measures that show whether an awareness programme works

cards.title: The poster problem
cards.setting: Learning and Development room, Rimal Bank head office, Riyadh. Monday, 9:00 am.

lines.text: Here is our current 'awareness programme': one e-learning module from three years ago and a poster in the lift.
The simulation results match. People who clicked had never seen a spear-phishing example aimed at our own executives.
My tellers want short, practical sessions. They can't leave the counter for half a day.
And my investigators need deep training, not the same slides as everyone else.
Then you have just described sections 3.1.6 and 3.1.7: awareness for everyone, tailored by audience, and specialist training for key roles.
Welcome to the Lantern Hall. Let's build a programme SAMA would recognise.

scenes.heading: The goal
scenes.narration: SAMA wants a risk-aware culture in which staff, third parties and customers make sound, risk-based decisions that protect the bank's information.

scenes.heading: Three audiences
scenes.narration: The programme must be defined and run for three groups: the bank's staff, its third parties such as contractors and suppliers, and its customers.

scenes.heading: Tailored and multi-channel
scenes.narration: It should target behaviour, be tailored to different groups and reach them through several channels. Activities run periodically and throughout the year, not once.

scenes.heading: Minimum content
scenes.narration: At a minimum it explains the security measures in place, the roles and responsibilities for cyber security, and current threats, with spear-phishing and whaling given as examples.

scenes.heading: Measured
scenes.narration: The programme must be evaluated to measure its effectiveness and to recommend improvements. Customer awareness must cover retail and commercial customers and suggest protective steps they can take.

cards.title: The awareness programme cycle
cards.caption: Section 3.1.6 asks for a programme that is approved, tailored, periodic and evaluated.

items.label: Define and approve
items.detail: CISO designs; committee approves the programme.

items.label: Tailor by audience
items.detail: Staff, third parties, retail and commercial customers.

items.label: Deliver all year
items.detail: Multiple channels, periodic activities, current threats.

items.label: Evaluate
items.detail: Measure effectiveness with tests, simulations and surveys.

items.label: Improve
items.detail: Turn results into recommendations and update content.

cards.question: Which audience does section 3.1.6 require the awareness programme to cover in addition to staff and third parties?
options: Only the board of directors
The bank's customers
Shareholders holding more than 5%
cards.explanation: The programme must be defined and conducted for staff, third parties and customers of the bank. Customer awareness covers retail and commercial customers.

cards.title: Awareness or training?
cards.prompt: Sort each activity into the section of the framework it mainly supports.

items.text: A quarterly email on a new whaling technique aimed at executives
A secure-coding course for developers who maintain the mobile app
Advice on the website listing protections business customers can use
A risk-assessment method course for staff who assess information assets
A short video for contractors on how to report a suspicious message
Incident-handling skills training for the cyber security function
A phishing simulation followed by a one-page explanation

cards.title: Section 3.1.7: specialist training
Who needs what
cards.prompt: Match each group at Rimal Bank to the learning SAMA's frameworks expect.

pairs.right: Cyber awareness at the start of employment, then throughout it
Specialist skills training linked to their job description
Skilled and continuously trained staff for 24x7 monitoring
Awareness on threats and protective steps through bank channels
Specialist training and defined professional certifications

lines.text: Our IT colleagues asked whether the cyber framework is the only one that sets training rules for them.
No. SAMA's IT Governance Framework of 2021 has its own section on staff competence and training.
So IT staff get it from both sides?
Exactly. Cyber skills from 3.1.7, IT competence from the IT framework. And people with continuity roles have a third source in the BCM framework.

cards.title: IT Governance Framework section 3.1.8: staff competence
cards.caption: The CIO defines the IT training plan in coordination with HR (section 3.1.5).

items.label: Identify critical IT roles
items.detail: For example database and system administrators.

items.label: No single point of failure
items.detail: A critical role must not depend on only one person.

items.label: Define certifications
items.detail: Name the professional certifications critical roles need.

items.label: Annual IT training plan
items.detail: Prepared each year, with the CIO and HR, and reviewed periodically.

items.label: Formal and specialist training
items.detail: For existing and new IT staff, contractors, and specialist roles.

cards.title: One course for everyone?
cards.situation: To save budget, Rimal Bank's HR team proposes a single 30-minute annual e-learning on cyber security for every employee, contractor and IT specialist, with no follow-up. They ask whether this meets SAMA's expectations.

choices.text: Keep a baseline module for all, but add tailored activities through the year, specialist training for the 3.1.7 groups, an annual IT training plan, and measures of effectiveness.
choices.outcome: Best answer. Section 3.1.6 wants tailored, periodic, evaluated awareness; 3.1.7 and the IT framework want specialist training for named groups; IT needs an annual training plan.

choices.text: Accept the single module, because the framework does not name a minimum number of hours.
choices.outcome: The framework is silent on hours, but it clearly asks for tailoring, periodic activity through the year, specialist skills training and evaluation. One module does none of that.

choices.text: Accept it for staff but run a separate technical course for IT and cyber teams.
choices.outcome: Better, because specialist training is covered. But awareness still needs tailoring by audience, activity through the year and evaluation of effectiveness.

choices.text: Replace training with a signed declaration that staff have read the policy.
choices.outcome: Declarations have a place, but they do not build skills or awareness and do not satisfy sections 3.1.6 or 3.1.7.

cards.back: Cyber awareness programme for staff, third parties and customers, run through the year and evaluated.
Specialist skills training for key roles, cyber staff, developers and maintainers, and risk assessors.
HR process: awareness at the start and during employment, NDAs, disciplinary measures, screening.
Critical IT roles, certifications, annual IT training plan, formal training for IT staff and contractors.
A training and awareness programme so staff and suppliers know continuity plans and their roles.
Fraud awareness for employees, customers and third parties, with knowledge checks for staff.

cards.title: Real case: SAMA's Cyber Anti-Fraud Program (2023-2024)
cards.body:
In **September 2023** SAMA announced the first edition of its **Cyber Anti-Fraud Program**: a three-month programme of intensive cyber fraud education and on-the-job training for a cohort drawn from SAMA and local banks, run with a British university and international specialist organisations.

In **February 2024** SAMA's Vice Governor for Supervision and Technology honoured the graduates in Riyadh. SAMA said the programme exposed trainees to international practice, real-world fraud scenarios and detection methods, including hands-on work with global banks, and described the fight against cyber fraud as a top priority.

**Lesson for you:** the regulator itself invests in specialist cyber and fraud skills, not only general awareness. When SAMA reviews your training records, expect questions about how specialist roles are developed, not just completion rates for an e-learning module.

*Sources: SAMA news releases, 19 September 2023 and 5 February 2024.*

cards.question: Under the IT Governance Framework, which of these is a staff competence requirement?
options: Critical IT roles must not be handled by only one staff member
IT staff must sit an external exam every quarter
Contractors are excluded from formal IT training
cards.explanation: Section 3.1.8 asks banks to ensure adequate staffing so a critical IT role is not handled by only one person, and requires formal training for IT staff and, where applicable, contractors.

cards.title: Make evaluation real
Lantern Hall: what to remember
items: Section 3.1.6: an approved awareness programme for staff, third parties and customers, tailored, multi-channel, run through the year and evaluated.
Minimum content: security measures, roles and responsibilities, and current threats such as spear-phishing and whaling.
Section 3.1.7: specialist training for key roles, cyber staff, developers and maintainers of information assets, and risk assessors.
HR processes give awareness at the start and during employment and bind staff to confidentiality after they leave.
The IT Governance Framework adds critical IT roles, certifications and an annual IT training plan; the BCM framework adds continuity awareness.

cards.prompt: Pick one group in your bank, such as tellers, developers or business customers. What would a tailored awareness activity for them look like, and how would you prove it changed behaviour?

quiz.question: What objective does section 3.1.6 set for the cyber security awareness programme?
options: A certificate for every employee before they use email
A risk-aware culture where people make risk-based decisions that protect information
A reduction in IT spending on security tools
Full transfer of cyber risk to customers
quiz.explanation: The objective is a cyber risk-aware culture in which staff, third parties and customers make effective risk-based decisions that protect the bank's information.

quiz.question: How often should awareness programme activities run under section 3.1.6?
options: Once at induction only
Only after a reported incident
Periodically and throughout the year
Every three years with the policy review
quiz.explanation: The control consideration says the activities should be conducted periodically and throughout the year.

quiz.question: Which threats does the framework name as examples of emerging threats the awareness programme must cover?
options: Ransomware and cryptojacking
Skimming and cash trapping
Insider trading and front running
Spear-phishing and whaling
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.6 requires information on relevant emerging events and threats and gives spear-phishing and whaling as examples.

quiz.question: What must customer awareness include at a minimum?
options: A list of suggested security mechanisms customers can use to reduce their own risk
The bank's internal incident reports for the year
Details of the bank's firewall configuration
A copy of the CISO's annual report to the board
quiz.explanation: Customer awareness must address retail and commercial customers and include suggested mechanisms they may implement to lower their own risk.

quiz.question: A developer who maintains Rimal Bank's mobile banking app asks which section requires her to receive specialist security training. What do you answer?
options: Section 3.1.6, which applies only to customers
Section 3.1.7, which covers staff who develop and technically maintain information assets
Section 3.4.1, which applies to vendor contracts
Section 3.3.13, which applies to ATM networks
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.7 lists staff involved in developing and technically maintaining information assets among the groups needing specialist skills training.

quiz.question: Under the HR subdomain (3.3.1), when should staff receive cyber security awareness?
options: Only when they are promoted
Only when they leave the bank
At the start of and during their employment
Only if they fail a phishing test
quiz.explanation: The HR process should ensure staff receive cyber awareness at the start and during their employment.

quiz.question: Under the IT Governance Framework, who defines the IT training plan, and with whom?
options: The CIO, in coordination with HR
The CISO, in coordination with SAMA
Internal audit, with the board
Each IT employee, with their line manager
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.5 makes the CIO accountable for defining the IT training plan in coordination with HR.

quiz.question: Rimal Bank has one experienced database administrator who alone runs the core database. Which IT Governance Framework requirement is at risk?
options: Keeping the IT budget within the board's limits
Logging every user request with a reference number
Approving changes through the change advisory board
Ensuring critical IT roles are not handled by only one staff member
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.8 requires adequate staffing so critical IT roles do not rest with only one staff member.

quiz.question: The awareness team reports that 98% of staff completed the e-learning. Why might the cyber security committee still challenge the programme?
options: Section 3.1.6 asks for the programme's effectiveness to be measured, not just completion
Completion above 95% must be reported to SAMA within five days
E-learning is not permitted as an awareness channel
Completion data belongs to HR and cannot be shared
quiz.explanation: The framework requires evaluation of the programme to measure effectiveness and recommend improvements. Completion alone does not show changed behaviour.

quiz.question: Under the IT Governance Framework, who must receive formal training as a minimum?
options: Only IT managers above a set grade
Only staff who hold professional certificates
Existing and new IT staff, and contractors where applicable
Only staff who joined in the current year
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.8 requires formal training at a minimum for existing and new IT staff and, where applicable, contractors.

sessions.title: Phishing, Social Engineering and Cyber-Enabled Fraud
sessions.summary: Recognise spear-phishing, whaling, impersonation and account takeover, and apply SAMA's counter-fraud rules on staff and customer awareness, authentication and immediate reporting of new fraud types.
objectives: Recognise the stages and warning signs of social-engineering attacks on staff and customers
Explain the employee, customer and third-party awareness duties in SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework
Apply authentication safeguards from the Counter-Fraud and Cyber Security frameworks
Respond to a suspected scam at the counter and know when SAMA must be told

cards.title: The caller who knew too much
cards.setting: Counter-Fraud Department, Rimal Bank, Riyadh. Tuesday, 10:30 am.

lines.text: Here's the Jeddah case. The customer got a call from someone 'from Rimal Bank security'. He knew her name and her last card purchase.
Hessa Al-Shammari, customer service in Jeddah. She came to my desk crying. The caller said her account was under attack and asked for the code we had just texted her.
That code was for adding a new beneficiary. Within minutes the money went out in several transfers.
Social engineering. No firewall was broken; a person was persuaded.
SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework calls this cyber-enabled fraud, often run by organised groups across borders.
Welcome to the Mirage Market, where nothing is what it seems. Let's learn to see through it.

scenes.heading: Pretend to be trusted
scenes.narration: The attacker poses as someone the victim trusts: the bank, SAMA, a government body, a courier or a senior manager.

scenes.heading: Create urgency
scenes.narration: There is always a reason to act now: an account about to be frozen, a prize about to expire, a director waiting for a payment.

scenes.heading: Ask for the key
scenes.narration: The real goal is a password, a one-time code, card details, or a payment the victim approves themselves.

scenes.heading: Spear-phishing and whaling
scenes.narration: Spear-phishing is a message crafted for one person or team. Whaling targets senior executives. SAMA's framework names both as threats the awareness programme must cover.

scenes.heading: The defence
scenes.narration: Stop, verify through an official channel you already know, and report. Banks never need your full password or a one-time code over the phone.

cards.title: From a message to a loss
cards.caption: Each stage is a chance to stop the attack: aware people break the early stages, bank controls break the later ones.

items.label: Bait
items.detail: SMS, call, email or social media post that looks official.

items.label: Hook
items.detail: A link to a fake site or a request to call back.

items.label: Capture
items.detail: Credentials, card data or one-time codes handed over.

items.label: Takeover
items.detail: New device, new beneficiary, higher limits.

items.label: Cash-out
items.detail: Fast transfers to mule accounts.

cards.question: A message says it is from SAMA and that the central bank is holding funds for the recipient, who should 'update details' through a link. Based on SAMA's own warning, what should staff tell customers?
options: Update the details quickly before the funds expire
SAMA does not hold deposits for individuals; ignore the message and use official sources only
Forward the link to the branch so a teller can complete it
cards.explanation: SAMA's 2020 warning said it does not keep deposits or money belonging to individuals and urged people to get information only from official sources.

cards.title: Real case: SAMA warns of messages using its name (2020)
cards.body:
On **19 October 2020** SAMA warned citizens and residents about fraud attempts in which callers and text messages used SAMA's name, or claimed to come from one of its employees.

SAMA said it had detected a number of fraudulent calls and messages that tried to obtain personal banking data. The fraudsters told recipients that SAMA was holding money for them, or asked them to "update" account information by calling a number or opening a **phishing link**.

SAMA reminded the public that it **does not keep deposits or money for individuals** and does not carry out transactions for them. The aim of such schemes, it said, is to steal money or to use the victim's account for illegal transactions. People should rely on **official sources only**.

**Lesson for you:** impersonation of trusted bodies is a standard opening move. Staff need to recognise it, and customers need the same message through every channel.

*Source: SAMA news release, 19 October 2020.*

cards.title: Red flag or routine?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation at Rimal Bank.

items.text: A caller 'from the bank' asks the customer to read out the code just sent by SMS
An email from the 'CEO' asks a finance officer to make an urgent, confidential transfer
A text links to a site with the bank's logo asking for card details to 'unfreeze' an account
A customer gets an SMS confirming a beneficiary they added themselves in the app
A login from a new device and country followed by a new beneficiary
The official app asks the customer to confirm a transfer they started
An IT 'support' visitor at the branch is not on the maintenance list

cards.title: What the Counter-Fraud Framework adds
cards.body:
SAMA's **Counter-Fraud Framework** (October 2022) applies to banks and must be read with the Cyber Security Framework. It opens by noting that small, individual frauds have given way to **large-scale cyber-enabled fraud** run by **international organised groups**.

Its fraud types include **social engineering** (credential capture and scams), **account takeover**, **impersonation** and **mule fraud**.

For people, it requires:
- **Employees:** fraud training at or soon after onboarding, refreshed regularly, with a **knowledge check**; those who fail repeat it. Branch customer-facing staff, managers with authority and fraud teams get **specialised training**. The board and senior management get training suited to their roles. Records are kept.
- **Customers:** awareness on current scams and how to report fraud, delivered through **all channels** the bank uses, with extra support for vulnerable customers and victims.
- **Third parties:** proportionate awareness, agreed in contracts.

When a new fraud type appears, staff and customers must be warned **immediately**.

cards.title: Authentication rules that defeat social engineering
cards.caption: From the Counter-Fraud Framework (4.4) and the Cyber Security Framework (3.3.13).

items.label: Multi-factor authentication
items.left: Not only an SMS one-time password
items.right: Add app approval, trusted device, location or behaviour checks

items.label: SMS one-time password
items.right: Sent in the customer's chosen language

items.label: Changing the mobile number
items.left: Only at a branch or an ATM
items.right: SMS alert to both old and new numbers

items.label: Wrong passwords or PINs
items.left: Access revoked after 3 in a row
items.right: Same for ATM cards after 3 invalid PINs

items.label: Unusual session
items.left: New device or location, risky IP

lines.text: Timeline of the Jeddah case: new device login, then a new beneficiary, then five transfers within the hour.
The framework lists exactly those as high-risk activities: new device, adding a beneficiary, unusual transfer rates.
And because this looks like a new pattern targeting our customers, the Counter-Fraud Framework wants SAMA told immediately.
What can I do at the desk next time?
Spot it, stop it, report it. Let's practise.

cards.title: At Hessa's desk
cards.situation: An elderly customer arrives at the Jeddah branch, phone in hand. A man on the line says he is from Rimal Bank's fraud team and needs the customer to read out the code he has just received 'to block a hacker'. The customer asks Hessa to help him read the small print.

choices.text: Calmly tell the customer not to share the code, end the call, check his account and recent changes through bank systems, and report the attempt to the fraud team at once.
choices.outcome: Best answer. A real bank team never needs a customer's one-time code. Fast internal reporting lets the bank protect the account and, if the pattern is new, warn others and SAMA.

choices.text: Read the code to the caller because he says he is from the fraud team.
choices.outcome: This hands the fraudster the key. One-time codes authorise actions such as adding beneficiaries; sharing one completes the attack.

choices.text: Tell the customer to hang up, but do not log anything because no money was lost.
choices.outcome: Stopping the call is right, but the attempt must be reported. The framework asks banks to notify SAMA of new fraud typologies even when there is no financial loss.

choices.text: Ask the caller for his staff number and continue if it sounds genuine.
choices.outcome: Fraudsters can invent staff numbers. Verification must go through a channel the bank controls, not through the caller.

cards.title: Respond to a suspected social-engineering attack
cards.prompt: Put Hessa's actions in the best order.
steps: Stop the interaction: the customer shares nothing more
Check the account for recent logins, beneficiaries and transfers
Report to the fraud team through the bank's internal channel
The fraud team blocks or restricts the account if needed
Counter-Fraud assesses whether SAMA must be notified
Give the customer guidance on spotting future scams

cards.title: Real case: SAMA's urgent anti-fraud measures (April 2022)
cards.body:
On **8 April 2022** SAMA announced urgent, temporary measures for all banks after a **notable rise in fraudulent websites and social media accounts** and repeated **social-engineering scams** in which customers believed they were dealing with official bodies and revealed passwords and verification codes.

The measures included **suspending remote account opening** and setting a **daily transfer limit of SAR 60,000** for individuals and individual enterprises, which customers could choose to raise.

On **12 April 2022**, after re-evaluation, SAMA restored the previous daily limit (customers could still lower it) and allowed remote account opening again under standard procedures. Both times SAMA urged consumers never to disclose passwords or verification codes and to use only trusted websites.

**Lesson for you:** when social engineering spikes, the regulator can change how every bank operates overnight. Front-line staff must explain such changes calmly and accurately.

*Sources: SAMA news releases, 8 and 12 April 2022.*

cards.question: Which control does the Counter-Fraud Framework set for multi-factor authentication?
options: MFA may rely solely on SMS one-time passwords
MFA should not rely solely on SMS one-time passwords
MFA is needed only for corporate customers
cards.explanation: Section 4.4 says MFA for identification or transaction verification should not consist solely of SMS OTPs and lists additional factors such as app approval on a trusted device.

cards.back: The victim is tricked into making or authorising a payment to a criminal's account, often after impersonation of a bank, investor or government body.
A criminal gains access to a customer's product or device to control funds or transact.
An account, often opened remotely, used to receive stolen funds and launder the proceeds.
A targeted attack on senior executives, named in SAMA's framework as an example threat.
A device the customer owns, controls and uses often; transactions from others get extra checks.
A fraud type not seen before; banks must tell SAMA immediately, even without a loss.

cards.title: Mirage Market: what to remember
items: Social engineering targets people, not systems: impersonation, urgency and a request for credentials or codes.
SAMA's awareness rules name spear-phishing and whaling; its fraud framework names scams, account takeover, impersonation and mules.
Employees get fraud training at onboarding and regularly, with a knowledge check; branch staff get specialised training.
MFA must not rely only on SMS codes; mobile number changes happen only at a branch or ATM, with alerts to both numbers.
New fraud types must be reported to SAMA immediately, and staff and customers warned straight away.

cards.prompt: Recall a suspicious call, SMS or email you or a customer received. Which of the warning signs from this stage did it show, and what would you now do differently?

quiz.question: How does the Counter-Fraud Framework describe the shift in fraud facing Saudi banks?
options: From small individual incidents to large-scale cyber-enabled fraud by international organised groups
From cyber fraud back to cheque fraud as digital use falls
From organised groups to lone insiders acting alone
From card fraud to fraud limited to corporate customers
quiz.explanation: The framework's introduction says small-scale incidents have been replaced by large-scale cyber-enabled attacks orchestrated by international organised groups.

quiz.question: Which pair of threats does section 3.1.6 of the Cyber Security Framework give as examples for awareness content?
options: Skimming and shoulder surfing
Malware and adware
Vishing and SIM swap
Spear-phishing and whaling
quiz.explanation: The framework gives spear-phishing and whaling as examples of emerging threats the programme must cover.

quiz.question: A finance officer receives an email that seems to come from the chief executive, asking for an urgent confidential transfer. What type of attack is this most likely to be?
options: A routine instruction that only needs the officer's own approval
A targeted spear-phishing attempt using impersonation of a senior manager
A denial-of-service attack on the payment system
A vulnerability scan by the internal security team
quiz.explanation: A crafted message impersonating a senior figure to get an urgent payment is classic spear-phishing; whaling is when executives themselves are the target.

quiz.question: Under the Counter-Fraud Framework, what must happen when an employee fails the knowledge check at the end of fraud training?
options: The employee is dismissed under the disciplinary policy
The result is reported to SAMA within five days
The employee repeats the training, and pass rates are monitored
The employee signs a declaration instead
quiz.explanation: Section 4.3.1 requires a knowledge check; staff who fail must repeat the training, and repeated failures lead to action such as re-training another way.

quiz.question: What did SAMA's October 2020 warning say about the central bank's relationship with individuals' money?
options: SAMA does not keep deposits or money for individuals or transact on their behalf
SAMA holds unclaimed deposits and pays them through text links
SAMA verifies individual accounts by phone each year
SAMA refunds scam losses directly to individuals
quiz.explanation: The warning stated that SAMA does not keep deposits or money belonging to individuals and does not carry out transactions for them.

quiz.question: Which temporary measure did SAMA announce for banks on 8 April 2022 in response to rising social-engineering scams?
options: A ban on all mobile banking for one month
A requirement for every transfer to be approved at a branch
Closure of all ATMs outside major cities
A SAR 60,000 daily transfer limit for individuals and suspension of remote account opening
quiz.explanation: SAMA set a SAR 60,000 daily limit for individuals and individual enterprises and suspended remote account opening; it eased both on 12 April 2022.

quiz.question: A customer wants to change the mobile number linked to online banking by calling the contact centre. What does the Cyber Security Framework require?
options: The change may be done by phone after two security questions
The change may be done only at a branch or an ATM
The change may be done by email with a scanned ID
The change may be done in the app with an SMS code to the new number
quiz.explanation: Section 3.3.13 says the customer's mobile number may be changed only from a branch or ATM, and an SMS alert goes to both the old and new numbers.

quiz.question: Rimal Bank detects a scam method it has never seen before. No customer has lost money yet. What does the Counter-Fraud Framework expect?
options: Wait until a loss occurs, then report it in the annual return
Inform only the internal audit committee at its next meeting
Notify SAMA immediately, since new typologies are reported even without a loss
Report it only if more than ten customers are targeted
quiz.explanation: Section 3.7 requires immediate notification to SAMA of any new fraud typology whether or not it caused a financial loss.

quiz.question: A session shows a login from an unknown device in a new country, followed by a transfer to a newly added beneficiary. What does the Counter-Fraud Framework require?
options: A third authentication factor to validate the instruction
No extra step, as the customer entered the right password
Automatic approval if the amount is below SAR 1,000
A delayed transfer with no customer contact
quiz.explanation: Section 4.4 requires a third factor for anomalous sessions and for transactions from a non-trusted device to a newly added beneficiary.

quiz.question: Through which channels should customer fraud awareness be delivered under the Counter-Fraud Framework?
options: Only the bank's website
Only branch posters and leaflets
Only channels chosen by the marketing team
All communication channels the bank offers to customers
quiz.explanation: Section 4.3.2 asks banks to deliver customer awareness through all channels offered to the customer, such as website, app, email, post and SMS.

sessions.title: Branch and Customer-Service Controls: Need-to-Know, Passwords and Quarterly Campaigns
sessions.summary: Apply SAMA's 2021 control and awareness measures for branch and customer service staff: passwords, need-to-know access, access logs, maintenance checks, three-monthly campaigns, six-monthly tests and yearly declarations, plus personal data basics.
objectives: Apply the password, access and logging controls in SAMA's 2021 branch measures
Use the need-to-know principle at the counter and in joiner-mover-leaver changes
Describe the awareness calendar: campaigns, tests, declarations and compliance reviews
Explain SAMA's instructions on protecting customers' personal data in general terms

cards.title: Sticky notes at the counter
cards.setting: Rimal Bank branch, Al-Khobar Corniche. Wednesday, 8:45 am, before opening.

lines.text: Welcome to my branch. Be honest with me: what do you see?
I'm visiting from Jeddah, and I see a password on a sticky note under that keyboard.
And a teller screen that shows every customer's balance, even for people who only update addresses.
We've always done it that way. The tellers share one login when it gets busy.
SAMA wrote a whole instrument for this in 2021: control and awareness measures for branch and customer service employees.
Welcome to the Counter Line. By lunch, this branch will look different.

cards.title: SAMA's 2021 branch and customer service measures

scenes.heading: What it is
scenes.narration: In April 2021 SAMA issued minimum control and awareness measures for branch and customer service employees of banks in the Kingdom. They sit alongside the Cyber Security and Business Continuity frameworks.

scenes.heading: Maturity first
scenes.narration: Banks must meet the maturity level those frameworks require, paying special attention to the controls for how branch and service staff use banking systems.

scenes.heading: Access and passwords
scenes.narration: The cyber policy must cover logins, identity checks, powers linked to job grades, strong passwords and restricted access based on need-to-know.

scenes.heading: Watching the watchers
scenes.narration: Banks keep detailed logs of who accessed customer account information, limit after-hours access from branch computers and check maintenance staff.

scenes.heading: Awareness rhythm
scenes.narration: Campaigns at least every three months, tests at least every six months, and a signed declaration when staff join and every year.

cards.title: Supervisory controls for branch staff
cards.caption: From the 'Third: Supervisory Procedures' part of SAMA's 2021 measures (translated text).

items.label: Passwords
items.right: Changed every three months; never shared

items.label: Failed logins
items.left: Three wrong attempts in a row
items.right: Username suspended until restored under bank policy

items.label: Access
items.right: Need-to-know: hide balances from staff who don't need them

items.label: Access logs
items.left: Name, job number, IP, time, action
items.right: Kept automatically for at least 5 years

items.label: After hours
items.right: Controlled exceptions when access is needed

cards.question: Under SAMA's 2021 measures, how often must branch staff change their banking system passwords?
options: Every month
Every three months
Every year
cards.explanation: The measures require passwords made of numbers, letters and symbols and changed every three months.

cards.title: Need-to-know in the branch
cards.body:
**Need-to-know** means a person sees only the information their task requires. The Cyber Security Framework builds identity and access management on **need-to-have and need-to-know** (3.3.5), and SAMA's 2021 measures apply it to the counter:

- A member of staff whose task does not require a customer's **balance** should not see it.
- Powers on banking systems are **linked to job grades**, and the minimum permissions are **reviewed periodically** and recorded.
- IT and support staff get access for **network maintenance only**, without access to confidential customer information.
- **Copying or sharing data or installing software** needs the consent of an authorised person.
- Screens are **closed or locked** when not in use.
- Maintenance technicians must be on the **approved list** sent by the responsible department.

The framework also expects **joiners, movers and leavers** to be driven by HR, so access changes when a teller moves to a new role and ends when they leave. Access rights are reviewed regularly, and there is an audit trail of requests and revocations.

cards.title: Control and purpose
cards.prompt: Match each branch control to the risk it reduces.

pairs.left: Hide balances from staff who don't need them
pairs.right: Snooping and leaks of customer financial data

pairs.left: Log name, IP, time and action for every access
pairs.right: Untraceable misuse; evidence for investigations

pairs.left: Restrict branch PCs after working hours
pairs.right: Unsupervised access when the branch is closed

pairs.left: Check the maintenance crew is on the list
pairs.right: Impostors posing as IT support

pairs.left: Suspend user after three wrong logins
pairs.right: Password guessing by an insider or intruder

cards.title: The awareness calendar for a branch employee
cards.caption: From 'Fourth: Awareness Procedures' and 'Fifth: General Provisions' of SAMA's 2021 measures.

items.label: Joining
items.detail: Signed declaration on secure system use and handling of usernames and passwords.

items.label: Ongoing
items.detail: Campaign on confidentiality of customer information and SAMA instructions.

items.label: Ongoing
items.detail: Campaign on information security and preventing financial fraud.

items.label: Testing
items.detail: Tests and surveys to measure whether the campaigns work.

items.label: Every year
items.detail: Renewed declaration, paper or electronic.

items.label: Oversight
items.detail: Internal audit or compliance reviews compliance with the measures.

items.text: Tellers share one login during busy hours
A security and fraud campaign runs every quarter with new material
Staff are tested once every two years
A new joiner signs the secure-use declaration on day one
A technician not on the approved list is allowed to 'quickly fix' a PC
Access records are kept for five years with IP address and action
Customer signatures on dormant accounts are visible to all tellers

lines.text: One more thing. Our account form asks every customer for their employer's address and their family members' IDs, even for a simple savings account.
Head office said 'collect everything, just in case'.
SAMA has flagged exactly that. It told institutions to stop asking customers for personal data that isn't necessary for the service.
That's the Personal Data Protection Law angle. We'll keep it at principle level, but every teller needs to know it.

cards.title: Real case: SAMA on unnecessary personal data (2021 and 2023)
cards.body:
In **December 2021** SAMA told financial institutions to bring their internal policies into line with the **Personal Data Protection Law** and the data governance rules of the **Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA)**, to carry out a **gap analysis**, and to present a correction plan to the **board** for approval.

In a follow-up circular in **late 2022 (1444H)** SAMA said it had **observed practices requiring individual customers to disclose personal data that was not necessary** before receiving a product or service, directly or through third parties. SAMA required institutions to fully protect customers' personal data, review those disclosure practices, build controls for the data's **security, integrity and use only for the purposes collected**, and report to SAMA on the measures taken.

**Lesson for you:** collecting "just in case" is a risk, not a safeguard. Every extra field is more data to protect and more to lose in a breach.

*Source: SAMA Rulebook, Adherence to the Personal Data Protection Law and Data Governance Policies, Regulations and Rules.*

cards.title: PDPL at principle level
The friendly cousin
cards.situation: A teller at the Al-Khobar branch is asked by her cousin, a customer of another bank, to 'just check' whether a mutual acquaintance has an account at Rimal Bank and roughly how much is in it. The teller's role gives her access to customer search screens.

choices.text: Refuse politely, explain that she may access customer information only for her job, and tell her manager if the request is repeated.
choices.outcome: Best answer. Need-to-know and confidentiality rules limit access to job needs, every access is logged, and repeated pressure should be escalated.

choices.text: Check whether the account exists but don't reveal the balance.
choices.outcome: Even confirming that a person banks with Rimal Bank discloses confidential information without a business reason, and the logged search would show it.

choices.text: Ask a colleague with balance access to check instead.
choices.outcome: This spreads the breach to a second employee. Need-to-know applies to everyone.

choices.text: Refuse, but not mention it to anyone to avoid family trouble.
choices.outcome: Refusing is right. However, a request to misuse access is a warning sign the bank may need to know about, especially if it recurs.

cards.question: Under the 2021 measures, how often must banks test or survey branch and customer service staff to judge whether awareness campaigns work?
options: At least every six months
At least every two years
Only when SAMA requests it
cards.explanation: The measures require tests and surveys of employees at least every six months to assess the effectiveness of the three-monthly campaigns.

cards.front: Sharing a login is fine if we trust each other
cards.back: No. Every action must be traceable to one person; the measures require staff never to disclose or share login details.

cards.front: Need-to-know is only for head office
cards.back: No. SAMA's measures apply it at the counter, for example hiding balances from staff who don't need them.

cards.front: Awareness once a year is enough
cards.back: No. Campaigns are required at least every three months, with tests at least every six months.
No. Support staff get access for maintenance only, without confidential customer information.
No. Declarations at joining and yearly come on top of training, campaigns and tests.

cards.title: Counter Line: what to remember
items: SAMA's 2021 measures set minimum controls and awareness for branch and customer service staff, alongside the CSF and BCM frameworks.
Strong passwords changed every three months, suspension after three failed logins, and no sharing of login details.
Need-to-know at the counter: powers linked to job grades, hidden balances where not needed, IT access without customer data.
Campaigns at least every three months, tests at least every six months, declarations at joining and yearly.
Access logs kept at least five years; audit or compliance checks compliance at least every two years.
Collect and use only the personal data a service needs, in line with SAMA's PDPL instructions.

A mix of numbers, letters and symbols
The employee's job number plus a word
Any phrase the employee can remember

At least five years

options: At least every three months
At least every six months
At least once a year
At least every two years

Only after a security incident

That the branch manager knows his name

An external auditor, only when requested by the board
quiz.explanation: The general provisions assign internal audit or compliance to examine compliance periodically, within a maximum of two years.

quiz.question: What did SAMA require of financial institutions after observing that customers were asked for personal data not needed for a service?
options: Review those practices, protect the data and report the measures taken to SAMA
Delete all customer data older than one year
Stop collecting national ID numbers at account opening
Publish customers' data rights in the annual report
quiz.explanation: SAMA's follow-up circular required full protection of customers' personal data, review of disclosure practices, controls for security and purpose limitation, and a report to SAMA.

cards.title: The night the app went quiet
cards.setting: SOC, Rimal Bank, Riyadh. Thursday, 11:40 pm.

lines.text: Lama, the mobile app login service is failing and the SIEM shows a credential-stuffing burst from thousands of IP addresses.
Classify it now. If it's medium or high, SAMA needs to hear from us immediately, not tomorrow.
Fraud alerts are up too: three customers report codes they never asked for.
A journalist is already messaging our branch social media page.
Nobody talks to the media until SAMA has been consulted. Priya, open the incident record and protect the logs.
This is the Watchtower: risk, incidents, continuity, and the evidence SAMA will ask for. Let's finish the quest.

scenes.heading: Identify
scenes.narration: List assets, threats, existing controls and vulnerabilities, and record risks in a central register.

scenes.heading: Analyse
scenes.narration: Judge the likelihood of each threat and its business impact.

scenes.heading: Respond
scenes.narration: Accept, avoid, transfer or mitigate. Acceptance needs business owner sign-off, must stay within appetite, be reported to the cyber committee and not contradict SAMA rules.

scenes.heading: Monitor and review
scenes.narration: Track the treatment plan and check that new or changed controls actually work.

scenes.heading: When to start
scenes.narration: Early in a project, before a critical change, when outsourcing is considered and when launching new products or technology. Existing assets are reassessed periodically.

cards.caption: The process is aligned with enterprise risk management and involves business owners, IT, cyber specialists and key users.

cards.question: A business owner wants to accept a cyber risk rather than fix it. Which condition does the framework set?
options: Acceptance needs only the CISO's verbal agreement
The risk must be within appetite, signed off by the business owner and reported to the cyber committee
Accepted risks must be published on the bank's website
cards.explanation: Section 3.2.1.3 requires sign-off by the business owner, acceptance within the risk appetite, reporting to the cyber security committee and no conflict with SAMA regulations.

cards.title: Incident management: what SAMA expects
Handle a medium or high cyber incident
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order SAMA's frameworks suggest.
steps: Inform SAMA immediately because it is medium or high
Contain it while protecting evidence and logs
Seek SAMA's no objection before any media statement
Send SAMA the formal incident report with root cause and impact
Feed lessons learned to the CISO and cyber committee

pairs.right: Inform SAMA immediately

Formal incident report to SAMA, including root cause and costs

pairs.right: Notify SAMA immediately under the Counter-Fraud Framework

cards.setting: Crisis room, Rimal Bank, Riyadh. Friday, 1:30 am.

lines.text: Branches open in a few hours. If the app is still down, customers will queue at every counter.
That's why the BCM framework expects a crisis management plan with clear criteria for declaring a crisis, a command centre and a communication plan.
And the cyber framework says cyber security must be reflected in business continuity.
We keep this at principle level today, but every branch should know its continuity contact and its role.

cards.title: Business continuity in general terms

items.label: Plans

items.label: Testing

items.label: Awareness

cards.title: The 2 am decision
cards.situation: Priya's team has classified the credential-stuffing attack as high. The head of corporate communications wants to post a reassuring statement on social media right away, before SAMA is contacted, 'to get ahead of the story'.

choices.text: Inform SAMA immediately, request its no objection for the statement, and keep customer-facing scripts factual until it is given.
choices.outcome: Best answer. A high incident must reach SAMA immediately, and the framework requires SAMA's no objection before any media interaction about the incident.

choices.text: Post the statement now and inform SAMA in the morning formal report.
choices.outcome: This breaks two duties: immediate notification and no objection before media contact. The formal report comes after operations resume.

choices.text: Say nothing to anyone, including SAMA, until the root cause is known.
choices.outcome: Waiting for root cause delays the immediate notification SAMA requires. Root cause belongs in the later formal report.

choices.text: Inform SAMA immediately, but let communications post the statement without waiting.
choices.outcome: Notifying SAMA is right, but media interaction about the incident still needs SAMA's no objection first.

cards.title: Real case: a SAMA circular on a new card fraud pattern (2021)
cards.body:
In **February 2021** SAMA issued a circular after noting that some parties were carrying out **suspicious point-of-sale transactions** by abusing the **pre-authorisation** feature and the later capture or purchase advice on cards linked to global payment networks.

SAMA told providers of acquiring services to follow the international card networks' rules for this transaction type, make it available only to the sectors it is meant for, **monitor** pre-authorisation transactions, **investigate** suspicious and high-risk ones by customer segment and amount, and build fraud monitoring and detection systems, in line with SAMA's earlier guide on combating financial fraud.

**Lesson for you:** this is the cycle the frameworks describe. A new pattern is spotted, intelligence is shared, controls change, and staff and systems are retuned. Your awareness programme is one of the channels that turns a SAMA alert into changed behaviour.

*Source: SAMA Rulebook, Financial Frauds Through Prior Authorization and Notification Features (circular, 1442H / 2021).*

cards.title: Evidence a SAMA reviewer may ask for

cards.back: Approved by the cyber committee, with audiences, channels, a yearly calendar and effectiveness results.
Proof of campaigns at least every three months and tests at least every six months.
Signed or electronic declarations at joining and every year.
Records for key roles, cyber staff, developers, risk assessors and critical IT roles.
Classification, SAMA notifications, media no objection, formal report, lessons learned.
Periodic reviews of permissions and five-year access logs for account information.

cards.question: Which document should Rimal Bank send SAMA after operations resume following a high cyber incident?
options: A formal incident report including root cause, impact and estimated costs
Only a copy of the press release
Nothing further if SAMA was told by phone
cards.explanation: Section 3.3.15 requires a formal report after operations resume, covering incident details, root cause, corrective actions, impact and estimated costs.

cards.title: Watchtower: what to remember
items: Cyber risk management has four steps, starts early in projects and changes, and needs business-owner sign-off for accepted risk.
Medium or high incidents go to SAMA immediately; media contact waits for SAMA's no objection; a formal report follows recovery.
The IT Governance Framework adds a detailed IT incident report within five days.
Continuity plans, crisis management and awareness of continuity roles complete the picture.
Keep evidence: approved programmes, campaign and test records, declarations, training records, incident files and access reviews.

cards.prompt: If SAMA's reviewer visited your team tomorrow, which piece of evidence from this stage would be hardest to produce? Who would you ask, and by when?

quiz.question: Which four steps make up cyber risk management in section 3.2.1?
options: Planning, building, testing and releasing
Detection, containment, eradication and recovery
Identification, analysis, response, and monitoring and review
Prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution
quiz.explanation: The framework documents risk identification, risk analysis, risk response, and risk monitoring and review.

quiz.question: When must the cyber risk management process be started, according to the framework?
options: Early in projects, before critical changes, when outsourcing is considered and for new products
Only once a year at budget time
Only after an incident has happened
Only when SAMA announces an inspection
quiz.explanation: Section 3.2.1 lists early project stage, before critical change, when outsourcing is considered and when launching new products and technologies.

quiz.question: How soon must a bank inform SAMA of a cyber incident classified as medium or high?
options: Within five working days
At the next quarterly meeting
Only after the root cause is known
Immediately
quiz.explanation: Section 3.3.15 requires SAMA to be informed immediately when a medium or high classified incident has occurred and been identified.

quiz.question: What must Rimal Bank obtain before speaking to the media about a cyber incident?
options: The external auditor's sign-off
SAMA's no objection
The approval of all affected customers
A court order
quiz.explanation: The framework requires the bank to obtain SAMA's no objection before any media interaction related to the incident.

quiz.question: Under the IT Governance Framework, within what period must a detailed IT incident report reach SAMA?
options: Within twenty-four hours
Within five days
Within thirty days
Within the next financial year
quiz.explanation: Section 3.3.8 of the IT Governance Framework requires a detailed incident report within five days.

quiz.question: Which item is NOT among the contents SAMA lists for the formal cyber incident report?
options: Root-cause analysis
Total estimated cost of the incident
The names of staff who clicked the phishing link
Date and time the incident was detected
quiz.explanation: The list includes title, classification, dates and times, assets, technical details, root cause, corrective actions, impact and cost estimates. It does not ask for named staff.

quiz.question: Which treatment option involves a business owner cancelling or postponing an activity that brings an unacceptable cyber risk?
options: Avoiding the risk
Accepting the risk
Transferring the risk
Mitigating the risk
quiz.explanation: Section 3.2.1.3 describes avoidance as a business owner's decision to cancel or postpone an activity or project that introduces unacceptable risk.

quiz.question: What capability must the incident management process include for major incidents?
options: A dedicated media spokesperson in each branch
A separate incident budget approved by SAMA
Automatic disconnection of all customer channels
Enough certified forensic staff, internal or contracted
quiz.explanation: Section 3.3.15 requires sufficient capacity of certified forensic staff for major incidents, whether internal staff or an external forensic team.

quiz.question: Under SAMA's business continuity framework, what does the crisis management plan need to include?
options: A list of all employees' home addresses
Agreement from every customer to service interruptions
Criteria for declaring a crisis, a command centre, a crisis team and a communication plan
A promise that no service will ever be interrupted
quiz.explanation: The BCM framework expects crisis criteria, command centres, a crisis team with contacts, defined steps and a communication plan that includes media response.

quiz.question: Customer and internet-facing services at Rimal Bank have not been tested for two years. Which requirement does this breach?
options: Quarterly penetration tests of all internal systems
Monthly external audits of the mobile app
Weekly SAMA approval of website changes
Annual review and penetration testing of customer and internet-facing services
quiz.explanation: Section 3.2.4 requires customer and internet-facing services to be reviewed and penetration tested every year.
